newsitem.title: USA: Jury gives largest verdict in RSI case.
newsitem.headline: Jury gives largest verdict in RSI case.

text.p: A federal jury Monday awarded a secretary more than $5.3 million for arm, wrist and hand injuries suffered from using Digital Equipment Corp. keyboards in what is believed to be the largest verdict of its type.

Plaintiff's lawyer Steven Phillips said it was the largest award in the United States for carpal tunnel syndrome, where the nerves swell at the point where they pass through the wrist. He said it was also the first monetary verdict for the injury in the New York area.
"This is the first major victory in keyboard litigation," said Phillips of the New York firm Levy Phillips & Konigsberg. "It is a break-through situation."
The verdict, along with smaller amounts given to two other plaintiffs, was awarded by a federal jury in Brooklyn after a three-week trial before U.S. District Judge Jack Weinstein.

Digital Equipment said it would ask Weinstein to set aside the verdict and that it may appeal to a higher court. The company said it believes its products are "safe and conform to all applicable industry standards."
"Digital Equipment prides itself on providing information to customers and employees about the comfort and safety in the use of its products," it said in a statement.

Carpal tunnel is among the most serious of repetitive stress injuries, muscular or skeletal disorders caused by the strain of repetitive motion that have affected thousands of workers in factories and offices.

Symptoms range from minor aches to disabilities so severe that some sufferers cannot turn door knobs, hold eating utensils or even a pencil. The pain can extend from the hands up the arms, shoulders, upper back and into the neck making it difficult if not impossible to turn one's head.
Phillips said that the federal Occupational Safety and Health Administration had fined Digital in 1989 for computer keyboard injuries suffered by its own employees.
He said that while the company took steps to improve its own work place conditions it did not warn customers about possible dangers.
The verdict could affect other cases pending against Digitial Equipment, Phillips said, estimating there were at least 50 other suits against the company in the New York area.

In the current case, the jury awarded Patricia Geressy, 50, of Staten Island, a former executive secretary with the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, $5.3 million for her debilitating injuries.
It also awarded former legal secretary Jill Jackson, 42, $306,005, and Jeanette Rotolo, 27, a former billing clerk, $278,000.

Phillips said there were 2,000 pending RSI cases in state and federal court in the New York area. His firm is currently trying such a case against International Business Machines Corp. in New York State Supreme Court.
